views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the September Washington talks on the calendar and use them to freeze the next rung of escalation rather than add new measures beyond the 23 August $75B retaliation already announced. Do not activate the unreliable-entity list or lean on a guided yuan slide as a bargaining weapon. Discuss agricultural purchases only as part of a package that delays or pares List 4 and restores a workable Huawei licensing channel — do not concede industrial-policy or enforcement language while the United States is still hiking planned rates and expanding the Entity List.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading sits at the high CHN anchor, not the existential one. Almost the entire U.S.-bound export book is now in the tariff crosshairs: List 3 has been at 25% since 10 May, and after the failed Shanghai round Trump announced 10% on the remaining ~$300B (List 4), then on 23 August directed a further 5-point increase (to 15%) plus threatened hikes on existing lists and told U.S. firms to “immediately start looking for an alternative to China.” Huawei remains on the Entity List; Commerce added more affiliates on 21 August and, as of 28 August, had granted none of 130+ license requests despite the Osaka pledge of limited relief — a firm-level hit on the national tech champion. CNY broke 7 on 5 August and was at 7.16 on 28 August; Treasury designated China a currency manipulator for the first time since 1994. Industrial production slowed to 104.4 (Aug), merchandise exports eased from the May/June peak, PPI slipped into deflation in July while pork-driven CPI rose, and official manufacturing PMI stayed below 50. That is major-export, FX, and Huawei stress. It is not financial-stability collapse: reserves are still ~$3.13T and essentially flat, IP remains positive year-on-year, and monthly exports are still ~$207B. Action should therefore not automatically escalate. China already matched List 4 with 5–10% duties on ~$75B of U.S. goods (soy, crude, pork) and the reimposition of auto tariffs, timed to 1 September / 15 December. Further unilateral escalation would be poorly targeted — the bilateral surplus means Beijing is near the limit of U.S. goods to tariff — and would raise the odds that Trump cancels the September round or hardens decoupling. U.S. pain is already visible (Michigan sentiment 89.8 in August, 10-year yield 1.47% on 28 August, VIX ~19), so a talks channel has leverage without new structural concessions. Concede_purchases or any rollback is premature: talks remain deadlocked on enforcement and on whether U.S. tariffs come off when a deal is signed, and Washington has not made a matching offer. Hold the already-queued retaliation; negotiate in Washington to walk both sides back from the List 4 / Huawei cliff.
key_factors: List 4 covering remaining ~$300B with 1 Sep / 15 Dec split and 23 Aug rate hike to 15%
Huawei Entity List still live; affiliates added 21 Aug; zero licenses despite 130+ requests
CNY through 7 to 7.16 and first U.S. manipulator designation since 1994
China already announced $75B mirrored retaliation including autos — little unused tariff ammunition
Domestic squeeze: slowing IP, PPI deflation, pork CPI, PMI <50, but reserves stable
September Washington round still scheduled; Osaka/Shanghai channel not formally broken
U.S. also showing stress (sentiment crash, collapsing yields), so talks have some leverage

sources_cited.excerpt: After the Shanghai round, Trump announces 10% tariffs on the remaining ~$300B of Chinese goods (List 4), effective Sept 1.
After CNY breaks 7 per USD, US Treasury designates China a currency manipulator (first such designation since 1994).
USTR splits List 4: List 4A effective Sept 1; List 4B (cell phones, laptops, toys, apparel) delayed to Dec 15.

China announces retaliation on ~$75B of US goods (5–10%, split Sept 1 / Dec 15), including re-imposing tariffs on US autos. Trump orders US companies to immediately start looking for an alternative to China and directs a 5-point increase on planned List 4 (to 15%).
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
CNY/USD latest 7.1628 on 2019-08-28, +6.8% over the window; broke 7 on 2019-08-05.
China industrial production index eased from 105.4 (Apr) to 104.4 (Aug).
China reserves excluding gold ~$3.126T in August, essentially stable (+0.4% over the window).
China SA merchandise exports $206.6B in August, down from the May/June ~$210.5B peak but not collapsing.
US Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 89.8 in August from 98.4 in July.
US 10-year yield 1.47% on 2019-08-28, down from 2.72% in early March.
China said it was forced to take countermeasures and hopes the U.S. will return to the Osaka consensus; talks were scheduled to resume in Washington next month.
Commerce received 130+ license requests to sell to Huawei; none granted as of 28 August. Only the temporary general license was extended.
Chinese officials sticking to plan to visit Washington in September despite August tariff escalation.
July PPI -0.3% y/y, first contraction since 2016; CPI 2.8% on pork/ASF — factory deflation plus consumer food inflation.
